lead: A thin-walled beam carries a transverse shear force S. That force does not sit at one point; it travels along the walls as a shear flow q, in N/mm. q equals shear stress τ times wall thickness t. The resultant of q acts through one point, the shear centre. If the load line misses that point, the beam twists as well as bends. Aircraft wings, fuselage frames and channel ribs are sized with this idea.
prereq: You need Unit 4 (second moments of area and unsymmetrical bending) and Unit 1 (wing and fuselage construction); see 5.2 for the full open-section calculation.

sections.h3: Shear flow is force per millimetre

blocks.text: Take a small element of a wall of thickness t (mm). The shear stress on it is τ (N/mm²). The force carried along one millimetre of wall length is q = τ t, in N/mm. This q is the shear flow. It is a force per length, not a stress and not a total force. For a vertical shear force S (N), q at a point depends on S (that is, on the rate at which the bending moment changes along the beam) and on the distance s along the wall measured from a free edge. At a free edge no shear can be carried, so q = 0 there. Moving along the wall, q builds up. A flange has nearly constant y, so q grows linearly along it and is largest at the web. A web has changing y, so q varies in a curve. At a junction the flow turns and continues.

blocks.where: q(s) is the shear flow in N/mm at distance s along the wall; S_y is the transverse shear force in N; I_xx is the second moment of area about the centroidal x-axis in mm⁴; t is the wall thickness in mm; y is the distance of the wall element from that x-axis in mm; s is the wall length measured from a free edge in mm. The sign gives direction; design uses the magnitude.

blocks.text: Every q element on the wall is a small force q ds. Adding these vectors round the section gives one resultant force. For a vertical shear S, the resultant is a vertical force of magnitude S whose line of action passes through the shear centre. For a singly symmetric section, the shear centre is where this line of action meets the axis of symmetry. A transverse load through the shear centre bends the beam without twisting. A load through any other point can be replaced by the same load at the shear centre plus a torque S × e, where e is the offset in mm. That torque twists a channel loaded at its centroid.

items: The shear centre is a property of the cross-section, not of the load.
For a doubly symmetric section, such as an I-section or a circular tube, the shear centre is at the centroid.
For a singly symmetric section, the shear centre lies on the axis of symmetry, but it may be offset along that axis from the centroid.
For a channel with flanges on one side of the web, the shear centre lies outside the web on the side away from the flanges.
Some syllabi call the shear centre the flexural centre; for the thin-walled beam model used here it is also the centre of twist.

blocks.text: For a plain channel of web depth h, flange width b and uniform thickness t, with flanges extending to one side, the offset e from the web centre line to the shear centre is given below. I_xx is the second moment about the horizontal centroidal axis. Measure e from the web centre line towards the side away from the flanges; a positive e in that direction means the shear centre lies outside the web, on the side opposite the flanges. The offset can be large even when the channel is small. A 120 mm deep, 60 mm wide, 3 mm thick channel gives e = 22.5 mm, while its centroid is only 15 mm from the web. Loading through the centroid therefore adds a torque. A lipped channel has small lips at the flange tips; the lips change I_xx and move the shear centre, and they also delay local buckling.

blocks.where: e is the shear-centre offset from the web centre line in mm; h is the web depth in mm; b is the flange width in mm; t is the uniform wall thickness in mm; I_xx is the second moment about the horizontal centroidal axis in mm⁴. The second form neglects the flange's own second moment.

blocks.text: The same integration method applies to any open wall: start at each free edge with q = 0, build q along the wall, take moments of q about a convenient point, and set the moment equal to S times the offset. The full distribution for an open section is worked in 5.2; closed cells are cut and balanced in 5.3.

figure.caption: The flow starts at zero at a free edge, grows along the wall, and its resultant acts through the shear centre. In the worked example q at the junction is 31.25 N/mm and e is 22.5 mm.

spec.title: From free edge to shear centre
spec.aria: A downward block diagram runs from a free edge where q is zero, through the build-up of shear flow along the wall, to the resultant vertical force of 5 kN and the shear-centre offset of 22.5 mm.

examples.question: A channel section has a web 120 mm deep, flanges 60 mm wide, uniform thickness 3 mm, and carries a vertical shear force S = 5 kN. Find the bending shear flow at the flange–web junction, and the distance e of the shear centre from the web centre line. Neglect the flange's own second moment about its centroid.
steps: Take x horizontal through mid-depth and y vertical. The web depth is h = 120 mm, flange width b = 60 mm, thickness t = 3 mm, and S = 5000 N.
Second moment about the x-axis. Web: t h³/12 = 3 × 120³ / 12 = 432,000 mm⁴.
Flanges: each area A_f = b t = 60 × 3 = 180 mm². Distance from x-axis is y = h/2 = 60 mm. Each A_f y² = 180 × 60² = 648,000 mm⁴. Two flanges give 1,296,000 mm⁴.
At the top flange tip q = 0. At the web junction on the top flange, y = 60 mm. q_j = S t y b / I_xx = 5000 × 3 × 60 × 60 / 1,728,000 = 31.25 N/mm.
Shear-centre offset: e = t h² b² / (4 I_xx) = 3 × 120² × 60² / (4 × 1,728,000) = 22.5 mm.
The shear centre lies on the horizontal axis of symmetry, 22.5 mm from the web centre line on the side opposite the flanges.
examples.answer: The bending shear flow at the flange–web junction is 31.25 N/mm, and the shear centre is 22.5 mm from the web centre line on the side opposite the flanges.

traps: Treating the centroid as the shear centre. In a channel they are far apart; a load at the centroid adds a torque S × e and twists the beam.
Using q = τ t with t in centimetres, or reporting q as a total force. q is in N/mm; multiply by a wall length to get force.
Starting the integration at a corner or junction instead of a free edge. For an open wall, q = 0 only at a free edge.
Taking the channel shear-centre offset towards the flanges. The shear centre lies outside the web on the side away from the flanges.
Confusing a singly symmetric section with a doubly symmetric one. The shear centre lies on the axis of symmetry, but not necessarily at the centroid.

quiz.q: Define shear flow and give its unit.
quiz.a: Shear flow q is shear force per unit length of wall. q = τ t, where τ is shear stress and t is thickness. Its unit is N/mm.

quiz.q: Why is the shear flow zero at a free edge of an open thin wall?
quiz.a: A free edge has no neighbouring wall to carry shear into or out of the edge. The shear stress must vanish there, so q = τ t is zero.

quiz.q: A channel has h = 120 mm, b = 60 mm, t = 3 mm, I_xx = 1,728,000 mm⁴ and S = 5 kN. Find the bending shear flow at the top flange–web junction.
A vertical load acts through the centroid of a channel, not through its shear centre. What deformation occurs besides bending?
quiz.a: The offset between the load line and the shear centre produces a torque S × e. The channel twists as well as bends, so the total shear flow includes a torsional part.

quiz.q: Where is the shear centre of a doubly symmetric I-section?
quiz.a: At the centroid, on both axes of symmetry.

quiz.q: For a singly symmetric section, where can the shear centre lie?
quiz.a: It lies on the axis of symmetry. It may be offset from the centroid along that axis.

quiz.q: Use e = 3b² / (h + 6b) for a plain channel with b = 50 mm and h = 100 mm. Find e.
quiz.a: e = 3 × 50² / (100 + 6 × 50) = 7500 / 400 = 18.75 mm from the web centre line, on the side opposite the flanges.

quiz.q: Why is it poor practice to load a channel rib through its centroid in an aircraft structure?
quiz.a: The centroid is not the shear centre, so the load creates a torque. That torque twists the rib, adds unwanted shear flow, and can cause early buckling or distress at attachments. The load should pass through the shear centre, or the section should be made closed.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real wing ribs and fuselage frames, shear-centre offset decides where fittings and load paths should sit. A channel loaded at its centroid twists; the same material closed into a box resists torque far better. Computer codes compute q(s) by summing over booms and panels, the method in 5.6. Search next for shear centre of lipped channels, shear flow in closed boxes, and Bredt-Batho theory.
